title: Calling Staff
summary: In many casual restaurants, saying すみません to get staff attention is normal.
do: Call clearly but politely if there is no call button.
avoid: Do not wait forever because you think raising your voice slightly is always rude.
whyItMatters: Service styles differ from restaurants where staff constantly check the table.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Many restaurants also have call buttons or tablets.
travelerTip: Look for a 呼出 button before calling across the room.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Do Not Pass Food Chopstick-to-Chopstick
summary: Passing food directly from one pair of chopsticks to another is avoided.
do: Place food onto the other person's plate instead.
avoid: Avoid transferring food chopstick-to-chopstick.
whyItMatters: The action resembles part of a Japanese funeral ritual involving cremated remains.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: People typically place shared food onto a plate rather than pass it midair.
travelerTip: If sharing, use serving utensils when provided.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Do Not Stick Chopsticks Upright in Rice
summary: Avoid leaving chopsticks standing vertically in a bowl of rice.
do: Place chopsticks on the rest or across the holder provided.
avoid: Do not use the upright-rice position casually at the table.
whyItMatters: The arrangement is strongly associated with funeral rites.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Restaurants usually provide a chopstick rest, wrapper, or tray area.
travelerTip: If there is no rest, follow the table setup rather than improvising dramatically.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Tipping
summary: Tipping is generally not expected in ordinary Japanese restaurants, taxis, and hotels.
do: Pay the stated amount and thank the staff.
avoid: Do not leave extra cash assuming it will be understood as a tip.
whyItMatters: Service charges, where applicable, are handled by the establishment.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Staff may chase after money accidentally left behind.
travelerTip: Some specialized tourism services may have different customs, so follow explicit guidance.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Avoid Spearing Food
summary: Spearing food with chopsticks is generally considered poor table manners.
do: Pick food up normally when possible.
avoid: Avoid stabbing food like a fork unless there is a practical need and the setting is very casual.
whyItMatters: Standard chopstick technique is expected in most dining contexts.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Some slippery foods can be difficult, especially for learners.
travelerTip: If you are struggling, asking for a fork is better than stressing yourself out.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Do Not Point With Chopsticks
summary: Pointing at people or objects with chopsticks can appear rude.
do: Set the chopsticks down or gesture normally.
avoid: Avoid using chopsticks like a pointer.
whyItMatters: Chopsticks are eating utensils and carry table-manner expectations.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may see people gesture lightly, but direct pointing is best avoided.
travelerTip: This is an easy habit to avoid without overthinking.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Gochisousama
summary: A common expression after finishing a meal.
do: Use it when leaving a restaurant or thanking a host if appropriate.
avoid: Do not worry if fast casual settings feel too rushed for a formal exchange.
whyItMatters: It acknowledges the meal and effort behind it.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Customers sometimes say it toward staff while leaving.
travelerTip: Even a quiet ごちそうさまでした can feel very natural.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Itadakimasu
summary: いただきます is commonly said before eating, especially in shared or home-style settings.
do: Say it if it feels natural; a small hands-together gesture is common but not mandatory everywhere.
avoid: Do not treat it as a religious requirement for travelers.
whyItMatters: It expresses appreciation for the meal and those involved.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Groups may say it together before beginning.
travelerTip: You can simply follow the people you are eating with.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Noodle Slurping
summary: Slurping noodles is accepted in many noodle shops, but it is not mandatory.
do: Eat in the way you can manage comfortably.
avoid: Do not mock people for slurping or force yourself to perform it.
whyItMatters: Local dining sounds and norms may differ from what travelers expect.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Ramen, soba, and udon shops can be lively and noisy.
travelerTip: You can eat quietly if you prefer.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Order Mindfully
summary: Ordering more than you can reasonably eat can create unnecessary waste.
do: Start with a manageable amount and order more if needed.
avoid: Avoid treating food as disposable for photos or novelty.
whyItMatters: Consideration for food and staff is valued.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Small specialty restaurants may prepare portions carefully.
travelerTip: This is practical courtesy rather than a demand to finish food when unwell or full.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Pay at Register When Expected
summary: Many restaurants expect payment at a register near the entrance rather than at the table.
do: Check whether a bill slip was left at your table and bring it to the register.
avoid: Do not assume every restaurant uses table payment.
whyItMatters: Payment flow varies widely by restaurant style.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may receive a small bill slip after ordering or finishing.
travelerTip: If unsure, ask お会計はどこですか.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Soy Sauce Moderation
summary: Soy sauce is usually used in modest amounts rather than poured over everything.
do: Pour a small amount and add more if needed.
avoid: Avoid filling the dish to the brim or soaking delicate food unnecessarily.
whyItMatters: It reduces waste and preserves intended flavor.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Small soy-sauce dishes are common at sushi restaurants.
travelerTip: Restaurant styles vary; follow the setup in front of you.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Using Oshibori
summary: A wet towel may be provided for cleaning your hands before eating.
do: Use it primarily for your hands.
avoid: Avoid treating it as a general cleaning rag for the table.
whyItMatters: It is part of common restaurant hospitality.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Oshibori may be hot or cold depending on season and venue.
travelerTip: In casual settings some people wipe their face, but it is safer for travelers to keep it to hands.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Sushi Can Be Eaten by Hand
summary: Nigiri sushi may be eaten with chopsticks or with your hands.
do: Choose whichever method is comfortable and appropriate for the restaurant.
avoid: Do not assume eating sushi by hand is automatically rude.
whyItMatters: Both methods can be acceptable depending on the sushi and setting.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: At sushi counters you may see both.
travelerTip: Sashimi, however, is typically eaten with chopsticks.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Serving From Shared Dishes
summary: Shared dishes may come with serving chopsticks or utensils.
do: Use serving utensils when provided.
avoid: Avoid repeatedly reaching into communal dishes with personal utensils when dedicated servers are available.
whyItMatters: Shared-food etiquette depends on the restaurant and group.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Izakaya groups commonly share many dishes.
travelerTip: Follow what your group is doing rather than inventing a rigid rule.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Coughing and Sneezing
summary: Cover coughs and sneezes and avoid directing them toward others.
do: Use a tissue, mask, or your elbow.
avoid: Do not cough openly toward people in crowded spaces.
whyItMatters: Basic respiratory consideration is valued everywhere.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Masks are commonly used when someone has respiratory symptoms.
travelerTip: This is common-sense hygiene, not uniquely Japanese.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Lost Property
summary: Lost items are often turned in to station staff, police boxes, or facility counters.
do: Ask staff quickly and provide a clear description.
avoid: Do not assume an item is permanently gone just because it disappeared.
whyItMatters: Japan has well-developed lost-property procedures.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Stations have dedicated lost-and-found processes.
travelerTip: For important items, note where and when you last had them.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

illustration.pose: asking station staff with worried expression

title: Police Box
summary: A koban is a neighborhood police box where you can ask for help, directions, or report lost property.
do: Approach politely and explain the situation.
avoid: Do not hesitate to use one for legitimate help.
whyItMatters: Koban are designed for local public assistance as well as policing.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: They are common near stations and neighborhoods.
travelerTip: Knowing the word 交番 is very useful for travelers.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: When Unsure, Observe or Ask
summary: Many etiquette questions are contextual rather than governed by one national rule.
do: Watch what people around you are doing or ask staff.
avoid: Do not let fear of making a small mistake stop you from enjoying Japan.
whyItMatters: Politeness, consideration, and local guidance matter more than memorizing hundreds of rules.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Even Japanese people check signs in unfamiliar places.
travelerTip: This should be Sakura's core etiquette principle.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Prepare at Checkout
summary: Busy checkout lines move quickly.
do: Have your payment method ready when practical.
avoid: Avoid holding up a long line while searching through many bags after the total is shown.
whyItMatters: Small preparation keeps shared queues moving.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Convenience-store transactions can be very fast and screen-guided.
travelerTip: You do not need to rush—just be ready.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Vending Machine Recycling
kana: じどう はんばいき
summary: Some vending-machine areas have recycling slots for drink containers.
do: Use them for the intended containers.
avoid: Do not treat drink-container recycling slots as general trash bins.
whyItMatters: The slots are usually managed for beverage packaging.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Bins may be labeled cans, PET bottles, or bottles.
travelerTip: Look at the opening shape and label.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Masks
summary: Mask use in Japan can reflect health, allergy, seasonal, workplace, or personal preference.
do: Follow current facility requirements and personal health needs.
avoid: Do not assume everyone wearing a mask is sick or that masks are always mandatory.
whyItMatters: Practices vary over time and by venue.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Masks remain a familiar sight in public.
travelerTip: Check current signs at medical facilities and specific venues.
contextNote: Health/facility guidance can change; follow current requirements.

title: Circle for OK/Correct
summary: A circle can indicate correct, acceptable, or OK.
do: Recognize ○ as the opposite of × in many Japanese interfaces and gestures.
avoid: Do not assume every hand-circle gesture has the same meaning internationally.
whyItMatters: ○/× are deeply familiar evaluation symbols in Japan.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You will see them on quizzes, signs, and TV graphics.
travelerTip: Sakura already uses this concept naturally in learning contexts.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Come Here With Whole Hand
summary: Using the whole hand is generally safer than crooking one finger at a person.
do: Gesture gently with the hand when calling someone over.
avoid: Avoid overly commanding finger gestures toward strangers.
whyItMatters: Whole-hand gestures can feel softer and less confrontational.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Friends may use very casual gestures, of course.
travelerTip: Tone and relationship matter more than one universal rule.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Crossed Arms for No
summary: Crossing the forearms into an X can signal no, prohibited, unavailable, or incorrect.
do: Recognize it quickly in shops and service situations.
avoid: Do not interpret it as personal hostility.
whyItMatters: The × symbol strongly communicates negation in Japan.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Staff may combine the gesture with だめです or できません.
travelerTip: It can be very useful even without shared language.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Hand Gesture When Passing Through
summary: People may hold one hand slightly forward while squeezing through a crowd, often with すみません.
do: Use a polite voice and move carefully.
avoid: Do not push through aggressively.
whyItMatters: The gesture helps signal intention and apology for taking space.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may see it on crowded trains or shops.
travelerTip: The words matter more than perfectly copying the hand position.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Head Tilt for Uncertainty
summary: A slight head tilt can show uncertainty, confusion, or thinking.
do: Read it together with facial expression and words.
avoid: Do not treat it as a fixed coded gesture.
whyItMatters: Body language is contextual.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may see it with うーん or どうかな.
travelerTip: It can signal hesitation without an explicit verbal refusal.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Japanese Beckoning Gesture
summary: A common beckoning motion uses the palm facing downward with fingers moving toward the body.
do: Recognize it as 'come here' rather than 'go away.'
avoid: Do not assume palm orientation means the same thing across cultures.
whyItMatters: Gesture conventions differ internationally.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Staff or friends may use a small downward-facing beckon.
travelerTip: Observe before imitating in formal situations.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Finger Counting
summary: Japanese finger-counting methods can differ from methods familiar to travelers.
do: Recognize that someone may fold fingers inward or use a different starting finger.
avoid: Do not assume a hand shape always represents the number you expect.
whyItMatters: Counting gestures are culturally variable.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Different generations and situations can use different methods.
travelerTip: For transactions, verbal numbers or a calculator are safer than relying on gestures alone.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Covering the Mouth While Laughing
kana: くちもとを かくす
summary: Some people cover their mouth while laughing, especially in a modest or self-conscious moment.
do: Recognize it as one possible personal/social style.
avoid: Do not treat it as something all Japanese women do.
whyItMatters: Gesture habits are shaped by personality, generation, and social expectations.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may notice it in casual conversation or media.
travelerTip: This is observational culture, not etiquette you need to copy.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Small Hand Wave for No/That's Fine
summary: A small hand wave in front of the body can soften a refusal, denial, or 'no, no, that's fine.'
do: Read the accompanying words and expression.
avoid: Do not confuse every small wave with goodbye.
whyItMatters: Japanese conversational gestures can be compact and context-dependent.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: It may accompany いえいえ or 大丈夫です.
travelerTip: If staff wave while saying 結構です, listen to the words too.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Finger Circle for Money
kana: おかねの じぇすちゃー
summary: A small circle made with thumb and index finger can refer to money in some Japanese contexts.
do: Recognize the possibility from context.
avoid: Do not assume it always means 'OK' or always means money.
whyItMatters: The same shape can have multiple cultural meanings.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Older or service contexts may use it more recognizably.
travelerTip: Context is essential.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Bowing While on the Phone
summary: People sometimes bow unconsciously while speaking politely on the phone even though the other person cannot see them.
do: Notice it as a cultural habit rather than something you need to learn.
avoid: Do not assume it is performed intentionally.
whyItMatters: Body habits can persist even without visual contact.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: This is common enough to be a familiar cultural observation.
travelerTip: It is a fun example of how deeply bowing is embodied.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Peace Sign in Photos
summary: The V/peace sign is extremely common in casual Japanese photos.
do: Use it if you enjoy it; it is playful rather than formal.
avoid: Do not treat it as required for Japanese-style photos.
whyItMatters: It became a popular photo pose and remains widely recognizable.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Friends, idols, tourists, and purikura users often use variations.
travelerTip: This is one of the easiest gestures to recognize.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Declining Alcohol
kana: おさけを ことわる
summary: You are allowed to decline alcohol.
do: Say 飲めません or 今日はやめておきます if you do not want to drink.
avoid: Do not drink beyond your comfort to 'fit in.'
whyItMatters: Health, religion, medication, pregnancy, preference, and safety all matter.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Many groups offer nonalcoholic options.
travelerTip: Your safety is more important than reproducing an old stereotype about drinking culture.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Arriving for Social Visits
kana: やくそくの じかん
summary: For a planned visit, being roughly on time is considerate.
do: Message if you will be significantly late.
avoid: Avoid arriving dramatically early when the host may still be preparing.
whyItMatters: Hosts often plan around the agreed time.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: A few minutes around the agreed time is normal depending on context.
travelerTip: For formal appointments, err on the early side; for homes, do not show up far too early.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Giving a Gift
kana: おくりものを わたす
summary: Gifts are often presented neatly, sometimes with both hands.
do: Offer the gift with a brief explanation or thanks.
avoid: Do not worry about theatrical formality for casual friends.
whyItMatters: Presentation can communicate care.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Gift bags and careful wrapping are common.
travelerTip: The relationship matters more than memorizing a script.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Kanpai
summary: 乾杯 is the standard toast at the start of many group meals or drinking occasions.
do: Wait briefly if someone is clearly about to lead a toast.
avoid: Do not feel required to drink alcohol; any beverage can participate.
whyItMatters: The toast marks a shared start.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Groups often raise glasses together.
travelerTip: You can join with tea or soft drink.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Omiyage
summary: Omiyage are souvenirs/gifts often associated with trips and sharing with others.
do: Packaged regional snacks are an easy choice.
avoid: Do not feel required to buy gifts for everyone you know.
whyItMatters: The practice is social but expectations depend on relationship and workplace.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Boxes with individually wrapped pieces are common.
travelerTip: For a casual trip, choose something easy to share rather than expensive.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Splitting the Bill
summary: Groups may split a bill evenly, pay individually, or have one person cover more depending on context.
do: Follow the group's plan.
avoid: Do not assume either strict splitting or one-person-paying is universal.
whyItMatters: Age, workplace hierarchy, and relationship can influence payment.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Friends often use 割り勘, while senior colleagues may offer to pay more.
travelerTip: Ask naturally: 割り勘にしますか.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Opening Gifts
kana: ぷれぜんとを あける
summary: Whether a gift is opened immediately depends on situation and relationship.
do: Follow the giver's cue or ask casually if unsure.
avoid: Do not assume 'Japanese people never open gifts in front of the giver.'
whyItMatters: Modern practice is varied.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Friends may open gifts right away while formal exchanges may be more restrained.
travelerTip: Context beats rigid etiquette lists.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

illustration.pose: holding gift and looking to giver

title: Pouring Drinks for Others
summary: In some group drinking settings, people pour drinks for one another.
do: If the group is doing it, you can participate naturally.
avoid: Do not treat it as mandatory in every modern gathering.
whyItMatters: Traditions around alcohol vary by workplace, age, and group culture.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Formal dinners may show more mutual pouring than casual bars.
travelerTip: If you do not drink alcohol, declining is completely fine.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Public Displays of Affection
japaneseTerm: 人前でのスキンシップ
kana: ひとまえでの すきんしっぷ
summary: Public affection exists in Japan, but highly demonstrative behavior may be less common in some settings.
do: Match the atmosphere around you.
avoid: Do not assume affection is taboo or that everyone follows one conservative rule.
whyItMatters: Generational, regional, and personal differences are large.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Hand-holding is common; more intense PDA varies.
travelerTip: Treat this as social awareness, not a prohibition.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Receiving Compliments
summary: People may respond modestly to compliments, but modern responses vary.
do: A simple ありがとうございます is perfectly acceptable.
avoid: Do not feel obligated to deny every compliment repeatedly.
whyItMatters: Modesty conventions exist, but over-scripted denial can sound unnatural.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may hear いえいえ or そんなことないです.
travelerTip: For learners, thanks plus a smile is safe and natural.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Bowing
summary: A bow can express greeting, thanks, apology, respect, or farewell.
do: A small nod or modest bow is enough for most travelers in everyday situations.
avoid: Do not obsess over exact angles or copy very deep formal bows casually.
whyItMatters: Bowing is deeply embedded in Japanese social interaction, but visitors are not expected to master every formal rule.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You will see everything from tiny head nods to deep formal bows depending on context.
travelerTip: Pair a small bow with ありがとうございます or すみません when it feels natural.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Thanking People
japaneseTerm: ありがとうございます
kana: ありがとうございます
summary: ありがとうございます is a reliable polite way to thank staff and strangers.
do: Use it naturally after service, directions, help, or a purchase.
avoid: Do not feel you need elaborate gestures every time.
whyItMatters: Simple verbal thanks are appreciated and easy for travelers to use well.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Staff may bow while saying thanks at shops and hotels.
travelerTip: A smile plus a small bow is plenty.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Using Sumimasen
summary: すみません can mean excuse me, sorry, or even a gratitude-tinged 'thank you' depending on context.
do: Use it to get attention politely, pass through a crowd, or acknowledge inconvenience.
avoid: Do not assume it is always a serious apology.
whyItMatters: It is one of the most flexible politeness expressions travelers will hear.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may hear it before a request, after receiving help, or when lightly apologizing.
travelerTip: If you only learn a few polite expressions, this one is exceptionally useful.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

illustration.pose: slight bow with one hand raised

title: Aizuchi
summary: Short listener responses such as うん, はい, そうですね, and なるほど show that you are following.
do: Use light acknowledgements naturally while listening.
avoid: Do not interpret every はい as full agreement.
whyItMatters: Aizuchi often signals attention rather than acceptance of a proposal.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Japanese conversations can contain frequent small listener responses.
travelerTip: This is one reason silent listening can sometimes feel less engaged than you intend.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Greeting Without Hugs
summary: Everyday greetings in Japan often involve less body contact than in many cultures.
do: Follow the other person's lead; a smile and bow are safe defaults.
avoid: Do not assume a hug, cheek kiss, or handshake is expected.
whyItMatters: Comfort with physical contact varies by relationship, age, and setting.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Friends may hug, but casual acquaintances often greet with little or no touch.
travelerTip: When unsure, start with a bow and let the other person set the tone.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Indirect Refusal
kana: とおまわしな ことわり
summary: A refusal may be softened rather than expressed with a blunt いいえ.
do: Listen for hesitation, difficulty language, or alternatives.
avoid: Do not repeatedly push after someone has clearly signaled difficulty.
whyItMatters: Softening can preserve harmony and reduce confrontation.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Phrases like ちょっと… or 難しいです can function as practical refusals.
travelerTip: Treat repeated hesitation as meaningful, not as an invitation to keep pressuring.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Maru and Batsu Gestures
summary: A circle can signal OK/correct while crossed arms can signal no, wrong, or not allowed.
do: Recognize ○ and × symbolism in signs, quizzes, and gestures.
avoid: Do not assume every crossed-arm gesture is hostile.
whyItMatters: These visual conventions are widespread in Japanese everyday communication.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Staff may use an arm-cross × when something is unavailable or prohibited.
travelerTip: Context still determines the exact meaning.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Personal Space
summary: People often maintain clear personal boundaries in ordinary public interactions.
do: Match the distance and body language of people around you.
avoid: Do not crowd strangers unnecessarily.
whyItMatters: Respecting space helps avoid making others uncomfortable.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Crowded trains are an obvious exception caused by necessity.
travelerTip: Context matters more than a rigid distance rule.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Yoroshiku Onegaishimasu
japaneseTerm: よろしくお願いします
kana: よろしく おねがいします
summary: A flexible phrase used when meeting, beginning cooperation, or asking for someone's goodwill.
do: Use it in introductions and cooperative situations when appropriate.
avoid: Do not force a single literal English translation onto every use.
whyItMatters: Its meaning depends heavily on social context.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may hear it at introductions, work meetings, lessons, and requests.
travelerTip: Think of it as 'please treat me/us favorably' rather than one fixed translation.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Comfort With Silence
summary: Brief silence in conversation is not automatically negative.
do: Allow pauses without rushing to fill every second.
avoid: Do not assume silence always means anger or rejection.
whyItMatters: Pauses can signal thinking, politeness, or conversational rhythm.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may notice longer pauses in formal or careful conversations.
travelerTip: Watch the whole context, not just the silence.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Eye Contact
summary: Eye contact is used, but prolonged intense staring can feel strong depending on the situation.
do: Use natural, relaxed eye contact and look away normally.
avoid: Do not treat 'Japanese people avoid all eye contact' as a universal rule.
whyItMatters: Comfort varies by personality, age, and context.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Conversation often includes softer, intermittent eye contact.
travelerTip: Aim for natural rather than performing a stereotype.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Pointing to Yourself
summary: People in Japan may point toward their nose or face when meaning 'me?' or referring to themselves.
do: Recognize the gesture so it does not confuse you.
avoid: Do not assume everyone uses it the same way.
whyItMatters: Gesture conventions vary across cultures.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may see a finger briefly point toward the nose or face.
travelerTip: This is a recognition tip, not a rule you must imitate.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Remove Shoes at the Genkan
summary: Shoes are usually removed before entering the raised interior area of a Japanese home.
do: Remove shoes at the entry area and step onto the interior floor without stepping there in outdoor shoes.
avoid: Do not walk onto the raised indoor floor in outdoor footwear.
whyItMatters: The genkan marks a practical boundary between outside and inside.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Shoes are often lined up near the lower entrance floor.
travelerTip: Watch the floor level change; it usually tells you where shoes come off.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Tatami Footwear
summary: Tatami areas are normally entered without outdoor shoes and often without slippers.
do: Step onto tatami in socks or bare feet as the venue expects.
avoid: Avoid dragging hard footwear across tatami.
whyItMatters: Tatami is a delicate traditional flooring material.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Ryokan rooms and traditional restaurants may have tatami sections.
travelerTip: Follow the footwear boundary in the room.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Toilet Slippers
summary: Some homes and traditional facilities provide separate slippers inside the toilet.
do: Change into them only for the restroom and remove them when leaving.
avoid: Do not accidentally walk through the home wearing toilet slippers.
whyItMatters: They separate restroom footwear from other indoor areas.

title: Shoes in Temple Buildings
summary: Some temple buildings require shoes to be removed.
do: Follow the sign, shelves, or staff instructions.
avoid: Do not enter no-shoe interiors in outdoor footwear.
whyItMatters: Traditional flooring and sacred interiors may require shoe removal.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Plastic shoe bags or shelves may be provided.
travelerTip: Wear socks you are comfortable showing on temple days.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Shrine Prayer Pattern
kana: にれい にはくしゅ いちれい
summary: A common shrine prayer pattern is two bows, two claps, prayer, then one bow.
do: Use it where appropriate, but follow the shrine's own instructions because some traditions differ.
avoid: Do not assume every shrine uses exactly the same ritual.
whyItMatters: Specific shrines can have local practices.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Many major shrines post illustrated prayer instructions.
travelerTip: If uncertain, observing respectfully is enough.
contextNote: Common pattern, but shrine-specific traditions may differ.

title: Temple Incense
summary: Some Buddhist temples offer incense for worship.
do: Follow the temple's method and place incense where indicated.
avoid: Avoid blowing the flame out with your mouth when local instructions say to wave it out.
whyItMatters: Incense practices are part of temple worship traditions.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: You may see people fan smoke gently toward themselves.
travelerTip: Not every temple uses the same incense setup.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Temple Prayer: No Clapping
summary: At Buddhist temples, joining the hands quietly is common; clapping like at a Shinto shrine is generally not done.
do: Pray quietly and follow temple guidance.
avoid: Avoid automatically using shrine clapping rituals at temples.
whyItMatters: Shinto shrine and Buddhist temple practices are distinct.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Visitors may bow, offer incense, and join their hands silently.
travelerTip: Recognizing shrine vs temple helps, but respectful behavior matters most.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Torii Gate Awareness
summary: A torii marks the transition into Shinto shrine space.
do: Enter respectfully and follow signs or local flow.
avoid: Do not treat the gate or sacred space as a climbing/photo prop.
whyItMatters: Shrines are active religious sites, not only tourist attractions.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Visitors may bow lightly at the torii, though practices vary.
travelerTip: You do not need to perform every ritual perfectly to be respectful.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Goshuin Etiquette
summary: Goshuin are calligraphic seals associated with shrine and temple visits.
do: Present a goshuincho where requested and follow the site's system.
avoid: Do not treat the calligraphy desk like a stamp-rally station when worshippers are waiting.
whyItMatters: Goshuin have religious and commemorative significance.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Some locations use handwritten pages while others provide prewritten sheets.
travelerTip: Rules and fees differ by site.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Punctuality
summary: Arriving on time is important for appointments and business meetings.
do: Plan to arrive a little early for unfamiliar locations.
avoid: Avoid treating the stated start time as the time to begin finding the building.
whyItMatters: Being late inconveniences others and can disrupt tightly scheduled meetings.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Business visitors often arrive several minutes before the appointment.
travelerTip: If delayed, notify the host as early as possible.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Avoid Talking Over Others
kana: はなしを さえぎらない
summary: Formal conversations may leave more room for speakers to finish before another person enters.
do: Use pauses and aizuchi to show attention.
avoid: Avoid dominating the conversation by repeatedly interrupting.
whyItMatters: Turn-taking can be more restrained in formal settings.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Short listener responses may occur while the speaker continues.
travelerTip: Aizuchi is not the same thing as interrupting with a new topic.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Business Cards
summary: Business cards are often exchanged carefully in formal professional settings.
do: Offer and receive the card neatly, often with both hands, and take a moment to read it.
avoid: Avoid immediately stuffing a received card into a back pocket in a formal meeting.
whyItMatters: The card represents the person and organization in Japanese business culture.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Cards may remain visible on the table during introductions.
travelerTip: For ordinary tourism you will rarely need this, but it is useful for work visits.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Handing Important Items
kana: りょうてで わたす
summary: Important items such as documents, cards, or gifts are often handed with both hands in formal contexts.
do: Use both hands when it feels natural and respectful.
avoid: Do not turn every casual object exchange into a ceremony.
whyItMatters: The gesture can signal care and attention.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: It is especially visible with business cards, certificates, and gifts.
travelerTip: For travelers, using both hands for a passport or card at a formal desk can feel polished but is not mandatory.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Names and Titles
summary: Japanese names are commonly followed by honorifics such as さん; professional titles may replace them.
do: Use the person's preferred form or follow introductions.
avoid: Avoid attaching さん to your own name.
whyItMatters: Honorifics signal social relationship and politeness.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Business introductions often include family name plus title/honorific.
travelerTip: If someone introduces themselves in Western name order in English, follow their presentation.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Polite Work Messages
summary: Work messages often use more formal language than casual conversation.
do: Use established templates or ask a fluent colleague if the stakes are high.
avoid: Avoid copying anime-style speech into professional messages.
whyItMatters: Register communicates relationship and professionalism.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Phrases such as お世話になっております are common in business email.
travelerTip: For learners, clarity plus politeness is better than overcomplicated keigo.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Business Gifts
summary: Small gifts may be exchanged in some business relationships, especially around visits or milestones.
do: Follow your organization or host's established practice.
avoid: Do not assume every meeting requires a gift.
whyItMatters: Business gift culture depends on relationship and occasion.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Regional sweets are a common low-pressure choice in some contexts.
travelerTip: When in doubt, ask a local colleague.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

illustration.pose: offering modest gift with both hands

title: Office Shoe Boundaries
summary: Some clinics, schools, offices, or traditional workplaces require indoor footwear.
do: Follow signage and the footwear system at the entrance.
avoid: Do not assume all Japanese workplaces require shoe removal.
whyItMatters: Building design and workplace culture vary.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Slipper racks or shoe lockers make the boundary obvious.
travelerTip: Let the facility tell you what to do.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Formal Bowing
summary: Formal workplaces may use more deliberate bowing than everyday tourist interactions.
do: Follow the host or colleague's level of formality.
avoid: Do not perform exaggerated deep bows without context.
whyItMatters: Business etiquette can be more structured than casual life.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Employees may bow when greeting clients or seeing visitors off.
travelerTip: A calm, respectful bow is safer than trying to calculate exact degrees.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.

title: Formal Seating Order
summary: Formal meetings can have preferred seats based on status and room layout.
do: Wait for your host to indicate where to sit.
avoid: Do not stress about memorizing every room hierarchy as a visitor.
whyItMatters: Seating can signal respect in formal Japanese settings.
whatYoullSeeInJapan: Hosts usually guide guests naturally.
travelerTip: Following direction is more useful than trying to calculate the 'best' seat yourself.
contextNote: General guidance; local signs and staff instructions take priority.
